newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia bull market seen running for next few weeks.
newsitem.headline: Russia bull market seen running for next few weeks.

text.p: Russia's runaway share market climbed to a new record on Wednesday and traders said strong demand from Western investors would keep the bull market running for the next few weeks.

The Russian Trading System (RTS) 24-share index rose 5.24 percent to close at a record 347.11 at close on Wednesday from 329.83 at Tuesday's close, the NAUFOR brokers association said. Total reported market volume was a strong $65.65 million.
"There's still a good flow of funds and broad-based demand," an analyst with Brunswick said.

He predicted prices would continue to rally for the next few weeks with demand focused on national power supplier UES, the RTS volume leader. UES rose on Wednesday to $0.2525 from $0.2335 at Tuesday's close.
Most of the money flowing in is being invested in just a handful of stocks, including Mosenergo, Surgutneftegaz, Rostelekom, and Gazprom.

But several analysts predicted Rostelekom may not continue to perform as well, with some pointing to uncertainty about the transfer of the government's stake in the long-distance operator to the state telecoms holding company Svyazinvest.
Traders said a shortage of shares coupled with the inflow of funds would keep pushing prices up in the next few weeks.

Western investors, anxious to jump on the Russian equities bandwagon, are pouring money into Russia, while some domestic investors are beginning to switch out of the government securities market, where yields on GKO discount Treasury bills have fallen to about 30 percent.

"The flow of funds has caused a sea change in the Russian equity market. Local investment instruments are being squeezed by the decline in GKO yields," Jim Nail, head of research at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said.

The market remains vulnerable to any major changes in President Boris Yeltsin's health, although it has climbed to new records and virtually ignored the bout of pneumonia he is currently recovering from as he recuperates from heart surgery.
But in the meantime the market seems immune to major corrections.
"Fund managers are waiting for a correction. When there's even a hint of a correction, they come in and buy, pushing up the market," Dan Rapoport, director of sales at Centreinvest Securities, said.
"There should be profit-taking, but so far I see no indication of it."
"The market as broken through every resistance level across the board. Resistance levels don't seem to count anymore," Deutsche Morgan Grenfell's Nail said.
But some of the top stocks may be pushing the limits of what they are worth, and money would start to flow down into less well-known stocks that offer better performance, Nail said.

Rapoport said newcomers to the market are still focused on the more liquid blue chips, while more experienced players are taking a closer look at less liquid shares, including some on the new RTS-2 second-tier market.

Traders said there is strong demand for second-tier regional utilities and telecoms, which have been undervalued. The Brunswick analyst predicted several second-tier oil companies, which have been overlooked in the past, may attract interest.
